content: Increased irritation and itching at the vaccination site can lead to touching, scratching, and potential contamination of the hands. To minimize these risks, the vaccination site should be covered with gauze, a semipermeable dressing, and a layer of clothing during direct patient care until the scab naturally separates. Dressings should be changed every 3–5 days, or more frequently if exudates accumulate, to prevent maceration caused by fluid buildup. Hand hygiene is critical and should involve the use of an alcohol-based hand sanitizer (containing >60% alcohol) after any contact with the vaccination site or materials that have come into contact with the site, and before any patient contact. Care must also be taken to avoid direct contact with the vaccination site or contaminated materials from the site. If purulent material is visible or the dressing's integrity is compromised, the dressing should be changed as needed. Designated staff should regularly assess the vaccination site for local reactions and vaccine take, reinforce the importance of meticulous hand hygiene to vaccine recipients, and document and report any serious adverse events following vaccination. When feasible, staff responsible for dressing changes should be vaccinated, although it is acceptable for unvaccinated staff to perform dressing changes if necessary. All individuals handling bandages must adhere to contact precautions, and hand hygiene remains essential to prevent inadvertent inoculation. In non-patient-care settings where close personal contact with children or others is a concern, the vaccination site should be covered with gauze or a similar absorbent material and further protected with clothing. Hypoallergenic tape should be used for individuals with tape hypersensitivity. The vaccination site should be kept dry, although normal showering or bathing can continue. A waterproof dressing may reduce the risk of autoinoculation during washing. If the site is uncovered, care should be taken to avoid touching it. After showering, if the site becomes wet, it should be gently blotted dry with gauze, which should then be discarded. If a towel is used to dry the site, it should not be used to dry other parts of the body. Alternatively, the site can be allowed to air dry before replacing the bandage. No salves, creams, or ointments should be applied to the site. Contaminated bandages and, if possible, the vaccination site scab (after it has fallen off) should be placed in sealed plastic bags before disposal in the trash to further reduce the risk of inadvertent transmission of the live virus contained in these materials. Clothing, towels, and other cloth materials that have come into contact with the site can be decontaminated through routine laundering in hot water. Administrative leave is not routinely required for newly vaccinated healthcare personnel unless they are physically unable to work due to systemic signs and symptoms of illness, have extensive skin lesions that cannot be adequately covered, or are unable to adhere to recommended infection-control precautions. The close contact required for vaccinia transmission to household contacts is unlikely to occur in healthcare settings. The FDA recommends that vaccine recipients defer blood donation for 21 days or until the scab has separated. Contacts of vaccine recipients who have inadvertently contracted vaccinia should also defer blood donation for 14 days after complete resolution of their complications. If a substantial number of individuals are vaccinated within a short period, the resulting donor deferrals could impact blood availability, potentially leading to serious blood supply shortages.
